# Commitment

`customer_support.obj.core.commitment` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> Something a named human promised a named customer, in their own words, outside any contract. "I will check with engineering and come back to you Thursday." It has three parts and needs all three: an ACTION (what will happen), a TIME (when), and an OWNER (who). Strip any one of them and what is left is a reassurance, which is a different and much cheaper thing.
It is the promise customers actually remember and the one no system tracks. Ticketing products model the contractual clock in exhaustive detail — start, pause, calendar, breach — and model the sentence an agent typed into the reply box not at all. So the organisation optimises the clock it can see, and the customer walks away describing the one it cannot.
The asymmetry is worth stating plainly, because it drives every weight in this file: a met SLA with a missed callback reads to the customer as a broken promise, every time, and no amount of contractual attainment repairs it. A missed SLA with a kept callback usually does not read as a breach at all — the customer was told, and being told is most of what they wanted. That is not sentimentality. It is that an SLA is something the company owes an account, and a commitment is something a person owed a person.


**The discriminator.** An SLA Target is a contractual clock the company owes and can be audited on; a Commitment is a time one named human said out loud to another named human. Only one of them is remembered as a promise, and it is never the contract.


Also called: `Promise`, `Callback`, `Personal SLA`, `Agent Undertaking`, `Follow-up`, `Action Item`


### Questions this object answers

- Did we do the thing we personally said we would do, by the time we said we would?
- Is this ticket about to break a promise that no SLA is watching?
- Was the break given notice, or did the customer discover it by us going quiet?
- Of the several things we said we would do, which one is the customer actually holding us to?
- Is a commitment on this ticket the real deadline, tighter than anything contractual?
- Does this agent, team or account have a habit of promising times that do not hold?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- NOT the contractual clock. customer_support.obj.core.sla_target owns start, pause, calendar and breach. This object has no pause condition at all, deliberately.

- NOT what the customer is owed. customer_support.obj.core.entitlement owns that, and it bounds what may be promised — a bound this object routinely and knowingly exceeds.

- NOT the work. A commitment to file a bug is not the bug_report, and closing the bug_report does not close the commitment; telling the customer does.

- NOT the thread the words were said in. customer_support.obj.core.conversation owns the wording; this object owns the undertaking extracted from it.

- NOT how the customer feels about the break. customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment owns that, and it is a consequence of this object rather than part of it.

## States

Initial `open` · terminal `kept`, `missed`, `abandoned`, `cancelled`

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `open` | Made, recorded, due time in the future. The only state in which the cheap fix — send the update early — is still available.  | — | Nothing is wrong yet, and this is the window in which almost all recoverable value sits. |
| `at_risk` | Due within hours and the move is still ours. The pre-breach window, and the highest leverage moment in the entire object: a message sent here costs nothing and a message sent four hours later costs an apology.  | `hours_since(commitment.due_at) >= -4` AND `hours_since(commitment.due_at) < 0` AND `thread.ball_in_court = us` | There is still time to renegotiate rather than apologise. |
| `overdue` | The promised time has passed. Note this says nothing about whether the customer knows — that is `notice_given`, and the two together are what actually determine the cost.  | `hours_since(commitment.due_at) > 0` | We are late. Whether we are also untrustworthy depends entirely on the next message. |
| `renegotiated` | A new time was agreed BEFORE the old one passed. The healthy failure mode, and the thing good support teams do constantly and quietly. Creates a successor commitment; does not edit this one.  | — | The promise moved with consent. Cost is close to zero on the first reset and rises steeply. |
| `kept` | We did the thing, by the time we said, and told them. Terminal and unremarkable, which is the goal. | — |  |
| `missed` | The due time passed without delivery and without prior notice, and we eventually engaged. The customer now has a story about us.  | — | A trust event. Recovery is possible and requires acknowledgement before explanation. |
| `abandoned` | Nobody ever went back. Rarer than `missed` and much worse — the customer was left to work out on their own that we were not coming. This is the state that produces cancellations that arrive without warning.  | — | The relationship, not the ticket, is now the open item. |
| `cancelled` | Withdrawn with the customer's knowledge, usually because the underlying need went away. A legitimate and clean ending, and distinguishable from `abandoned` only by whether anyone said so out loud.  | — |  |

## Preconditions

- **`commitment.requires_a_named_time`** A commitment cannot be resolved without a stated time. Without one there is nothing to be early or late against and every downstream pattern is undefined.
 _(unmet → degrade — do NOT block and do NOT invent a default. Record it as a commitment that was never made, surface the missing date to the agent as an unfinished sentence they can close in the same reply, and keep it out of the promise-keeping denominator. Blocking would drop the record entirely and lose the capture gap, which is the actual finding.
)_
- **`commitment.requires_a_named_owner`** One accountable human. A promise assigned to a team is a promise assigned to nobody. _(unmet → block — refuse to open the commitment. This is the one precondition worth blocking on, because an unowned promise fails silently and is discovered only when the customer quotes it back, at which point nothing can be recovered.
)_
- **`commitment.requires_a_named_recipient`** A promise is made to a person, not to a logo. The recipient is who remembers it. _(unmet → degrade — fall back to the ticket requester, and mark the attribution as inferred. Wrong-person attribution is recoverable; no attribution means the promise cannot be re-made when the recipient leaves.
)_
- **`commitment.requires_an_observable_thread`** Every executable pattern here reads the correspondence. On a node with no ingested thread, the object degrades to whatever the due date alone can say.
 _(unmet → degrade — keep the arithmetic patterns (overdue, at-risk) and suppress every pattern that reads followup_sent or ball_in_court, rather than reporting confident silence. Reporting "nothing was sent" on a thread we cannot see is the worst available answer.
)_


## Constraints

- **`commitment.exactly_one_owner`** One named human owns a commitment at any moment. Reassignment transfers it; it never shares it.
- **`commitment.due_at_is_immutable`** The stated time cannot be edited. A new time is a new commitment that supersedes this one.

- **`commitment.has_no_pause_condition`** A commitment cannot be paused, for any reason, including out-of-hours, awaiting-customer and awaiting-engineering.

- **`commitment.cannot_be_closed_by_an_automated_message`** An autoresponder, a macro or a status-page update does not close a commitment.
- **`commitment.notice_must_precede_the_due_time`** Notice given after the due time is an apology, not notice, and must not set notice_given.

- **`commitment.may_not_be_promised_beyond_entitlement`** A commitment should not undertake more than the entitlement covers. _(soft)_


## Business rules

- **`commitment.no_named_time_no_commitment`** An undertaking with no stated time is not opened as a commitment. It is recorded as one that was never made, and the missing date is surfaced to the agent.
 — _A live promise with no due date can never be late, never be checked and never be discharged. It degrades the metric it sits in and gives false comfort that the promise is being tracked.
_
- **`commitment.silence_past_due_is_a_break`** A commitment whose time has passed with nothing observed outbound is a broken promise regardless of SLA state, and must be flagged as such.
 — _Customers forgive slow far more readily than they forgive silence after a specific date was named. Warning rather than blocking because the observation can be wrong — the reply may have gone by phone — and a blocking rule on an uncertain observation gets disabled within a fortnight.
_
- **`commitment.renegotiate_before_not_after`** While the due time is still ahead and the move is ours, a reset or a holding update is required rather than optional.
 — _This is the whole of de-escalation compressed into one rule. The identical information — "it is going to take longer" — is received as professionalism before the due time and as an excuse after it, and the cost difference between those two receptions is larger than anything else support controls at zero marginal cost.
_
- **`commitment.the_clock_does_not_pause`** No pause, exclusion or business-calendar adjustment may be applied to a commitment. — _The customer's Thursday does not observe our business calendar, our holidays or our engineering backlog.
_
- **`commitment.owner_is_a_person`** A commitment may not be owned by a queue, a team, an alias or a shift.
- **`commitment.an_autoresponder_does_not_close_the_loop`** A commitment may not be moved to kept by an automated, templated or bulk message. Closing it requires a message that addresses what was specifically promised.

- **`commitment.lead_with_the_promise_not_the_clock`** When a met SLA and a missed commitment are both true, customer-facing communication must lead with the missed commitment. Opening with contractual attainment reads as an excuse and converts a recoverable slip into an escalation.
 — _The customer's account of what happened is organised around what a person told them, not around what the contract said. Answering the wrong one is how technically correct responses make things worse.
_


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **"Thursday, once you send me the logs." The clock never started, so Thursday passing is not a break — it is a chase.
** — By far the most common shape of a support promise and by far the most common false accusation an overdue detector makes. Suppress the breach, keep the obligation: the right output is "chase them", not "nothing to do".
 _(overrides commitment.due_time_has_passed, commitment.missed_in_silence, commitment.silence_past_due_is_a_break)_
- **The agent called instead of writing. Every silence-based pattern reports a broken promise on a promise that was kept, by an agent who chose the better channel.
** — Phone and chat are not ingested, so the response most appropriate to a slipping promise is also the one most invisible to the detector. Worth living with — an unnecessary "did you get back to them?" is cheap — but it must be stated, because a team that handles promises well by phone will see the most false alerts and lose faith fastest.
 _(overrides commitment.missed_in_silence, commitment.abandoned_past_the_trust_horizon)_
- **"No rush, next week is fine." The due date is dead by agreement and every pattern here is still counting against it.
** — Release is stated in ordinary language in the thread and extracted by nothing. It is the mirror of `commitment_renegotiated` — a reset initiated by the customer rather than by us — and it is why an agent's first instinct on seeing an overdue alert is often "yes, I know, they told me not to worry".
 _(overrides commitment.due_time_has_passed, commitment.abandoned_past_the_trust_horizon)_
- **"I don't have a date for the fix and I won't invent one — I'll update you Friday regardless." This has no resolution time and IS a commitment, because the update has a time.
** — The single best move in the entire discipline, and the doctrine of this object reads it as a non-commitment if applied carelessly. Promise the speaking, never the fixing: the agent controls one and not the other. The rule survives, correctly read — the promise being tracked is the update, and the update has a named time.
 _(overrides commitment.an_action_with_no_named_time_is_not_a_commitment, commitment.no_named_time_no_commitment)_
- **"Hourly updates until resolved", said once to four hundred customers. One operational commitment, four hundred remembered ones.
** — Per-customer promise tracking during a major incident generates hundreds of identical critical alerts and drowns the incident it is supposed to be helping with. Track it once against the incident and fan out the status. The exception ends the moment the incident does — the individual follow-ups afterwards are real individual commitments and are routinely the part that gets dropped.
 _(overrides commitment.missed_in_silence, commitment.abandoned_past_the_trust_horizon)_
- **A promise due at 23:00 in the customer's timezone, kept at 23:00. Technically on time, experienced as nothing at all, and the reply is read the next morning anyway.
** — Meeting the arithmetic while missing the working day is a way of being precisely and uselessly correct. If the promise cannot be kept inside the recipient's working hours, it is better renegotiated to the next morning than technically satisfied overnight — and a system that scores only the timestamp will actively teach the wrong behaviour.
 _(overrides commitment.due_time_has_passed)_


## Best practices

- **Commit to when you will speak, not to when it will be fixed.** — You control one and not the other. An update promise is nearly always keepable, which means keeping it is nearly free, which means trust compounds instead of eroding.

- **Name the time you are confident of, not the time you hope for, then deliver early.** — Optimistic dates are made to relieve the discomfort of the current conversation and are paid for by a worse future one. Early delivery on a conservative date reads as competence; on-time delivery on an optimistic one reads as normal.

- **Send the update when you said you would, especially when you have nothing to report.** — Agents skip this believing an empty update wastes the customer's time. The customer reads the silence as being forgotten. "No news yet, still with engineering, next update Thursday" costs ninety seconds and preserves everything.

- **Move the date before it passes. Never after.** — The identical sentence is professionalism at T-4 hours and an excuse at T+1 hour. This is the largest behaviour change available to a support organisation at zero marginal cost.

- **Confirm the promise in writing using the customer's own phrasing and an explicit date, not a relative one.
** — "By Thursday 5pm your time" cannot be misremembered; "early next week" is remembered as Monday morning by them and meant as Tuesday evening by us. Writing it also forces the promiser to notice their own hedging.

- **Hand the promise over by name at shift end, separately from handing over the ticket.** — Everyone assumes the promise travels with the ticket and it does not — the ticket has a queue and the promise had a person. This is the dominant origin of dropped callbacks in follow-the-sun and swarming operations.

- **When a customer quotes a promise we have no record of, assume it was made and act on it.
** — Our record is systematically incomplete in exactly the direction that flatters us — phone and call promises are the ones missing. Arguing costs the relationship and wins nothing; the dispute is also the cheapest available detector of the capture gap.



## Anti-patterns

- **Naming a date on a difficult call purely to make the call stop being difficult.** — tempting because It works instantly. The customer calms down the moment a specific day is named, the call ends well, and the entire cost lands on a future self who has no idea it is coming.
 Instead: Name a time for the UPDATE rather than for the outcome, and say plainly that you do not yet have a date for the fix. It de-escalates almost as well and it is keepable.

- **Letting the promised time pass because there is still nothing to report.** — tempting because Sending an update with no answer feels like admitting failure and wasting the customer's time, and agents are trained to be useful. Silence feels neutral. It is not — it is the most negative signal available.
 Instead: Send the empty update on the date, with the next date attached.
- **Resetting the date after it has passed rather than before.** — tempting because Hope. Right up until the deadline there is a plausible chance the answer arrives, and pre-warning feels like giving up on it a few hours early.
 Instead: Warn at the point the slip becomes more likely than not, which is almost always hours earlier than it feels.
- **Recording the promise against a queue, a rota or a shared alias rather than a person.** — tempting because The promiser goes off shift and handing it to the team genuinely feels more robust than leaving it with someone who is asleep. It reads as coverage.
 Instead: Name the receiving human at handover and tell the customer who now has it.
- **Storing the promise in the ticketing system's SLA machinery because that is the only date field with a clock behind it.
** — tempting because Entirely reasonable engineering. The SLA subsystem already has due dates, reminders and breach reporting; building a second clock looks like duplication.
 Instead: A separate object with no pause condition. That is the whole architectural argument for this file existing.

- **Counting any outbound message as having closed the loop.** — tempting because The observation fires and the metric moves. From an instrumentation point of view an autoresponder, a bulk incident notice and a real personal update are indistinguishable.
 Instead: Require the closing message to reference the specific undertaking. Where that cannot be enforced, report the keep-rate beside the reopen and detractor rates so the divergence shows.



## Dependencies

- `customer_support.obj.core.requester` — requires (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.support_agent` — requires (hard)
- `customer_support.obj.core.conversation` — derived_from (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.ticket` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement` — enriches (soft)
- `customer_support.obj.core.escalation` — invalidated_by (soft)


## Inputs

- **email** — promises made in writing and the time named in them
- **email** — what was undertaken
- **email** — who is waiting on whom
- **email** — the customer's last message
- **calendar** — calls on this thread, as a proxy for verbal promises
- **derived** — observation balance across the thread
- **phone** — what was actually promised on the call
- **meeting_transcript** — verbatim undertakings made verbally
- **chat** — promises made in a widget session that no ticket recorded
- **ticket** — recorded follow-up tasks, due dates and owners


## Outputs

- **`promise_state`** open | at_risk | overdue | renegotiated | kept | missed | abandoned. The one-word answer to "did we do what we said". → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker
- **`silent_break_flag`** True when the time passed, nothing went out, and the customer has not been told. The highest-priority boolean this brain currently produces, and the one worth interrupting a human for.
 → L4.decision_maker, L5.communication_planning
- **`hours_past_due`** Wall clock beyond the promised time, unpaused. The number the customer is counting. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`renegotiation_window_open`** True while the due time is still ahead. The window in which a reset costs nothing, and the only output here that supports a cheap action rather than an expensive one.
 → L5.execution_planning, L5.communication_planning
- **`next_customer_message`** What must be said next and by when, given what was already promised and whether the customer has been told. Where a commitment and an SLA disagree, this leads with the commitment.
 → L5.2.channel_planner, L5.communication_planning
- **`trust_debt_bp`** Accumulated cost of broken promises on this relationship, in basis points. Distinct from sentiment: sentiment recovers on a good interaction, trust debt does not clear until a promise is kept.
 → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`promiser_reliability_signal`** Per-agent kept-versus-named rate, for coaching. Never for ranking without promise_type held constant. → L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`commitment.made`** Commitment Made
- **`commitment.due_soon`** Commitment Due Soon
- **`commitment.overdue`** Commitment Overdue — invalidates is_tighter_than_sla
- **`commitment.missed_silently`** Promise Broken Without Notice
- **`commitment.abandoned`** Promise Abandoned — invalidates trust_cost, promise_keep_rate
- **`commitment.renegotiated`** Commitment Reset With Notice
- **`commitment.kept`** Commitment Kept


## Actions

- **Record the promise the moment it is made** (agent) — Captures action, time, owner and recipient. The whole discipline in one step: an unrecorded commitment is an unmade one right up until the customer quotes it back.

- **Repeat it back in writing with the date** (agent) — Converts a verbal promise into evidence and forces the vagueness out — writing "Thursday" makes an agent notice they meant "probably Thursday", which is the moment to say so.

- **Send an update on the due date even with no news** (agent) — The single most underused move in support. Agents suppress it because an update containing no answer feels like wasting the customer's time; the customer reads its absence as having been forgotten, which is far worse than being told there is no news.

- **Agree a new time before the old one lapses** (agent) — Creates a successor commitment and preserves the chain. Nearly free on the first use and steeply more expensive on the third, which is exactly why the count is tracked.

- **Acknowledge the missed promise before explaining it** (agent) — Order matters more than content. Acknowledgement first, then cause, then the new date. Leading with the reason — even a completely legitimate one — is heard as a defence and makes the second promise less credible than the first.

- **Chase what the promise was waiting on** (agent) — A promise blocked on the customer is not our breach, but it is still our problem. Left alone it becomes a promise everyone has forgotten and the customer remembers.

- **Hand the promise over at end of shift** (human) — Moves the owner and keeps the speaker on the record. The unhanded-over promise at shift end is the classic origin of a dropped callback in a follow-the-sun operation, and it fails silently because everyone assumes it went with the ticket.

- **Withdraw the promise explicitly** (agent) — A clean ending. The only thing that distinguishes cancelled from abandoned is that somebody said so out loud, and from the customer's side that distinction is total.



## Evidence

- **email** · 9000 bp — The promise in the agent's own typed words, timestamped. The best evidence this domain has for anything, and unusually here it is also the primary record rather than a proxy — for a written commitment, the email IS the commitment.

- **meeting_transcript** · 8500 bp — The only thing that can settle what was actually said on a call. Rare, and where it exists it converts the domain's weakest evidence channel into its second strongest.

- **ticket** · 8000 bp — A recorded follow-up task with a due date and an owner. Strong when it exists, and it usually does not — most systems have an SLA field and no commitment field, so the promise degrades to a free-text note.

- **chat** · 7000 bp — Verbatim and timestamped, but sessions end abruptly and the promise is frequently in the last message before the customer closed the window.

- **phone** · 4500 bp — Where most commitments are made and almost none survive. What was promised exists only in whatever the agent typed afterwards, written by the person the record will be used to judge.

- **manual_entry** · 4000 bp — The agent's own note. Honest, unverifiable, and systematically kinder to the writer than a transcript would be — not from dishonesty but because people remember hedging they did not actually say out loud.

- **derived** · 3500 bp — Inferred from conversation shape — followups observed, ball in court, tone. Corroborating only. It can establish that nothing was SEEN to be sent, never that nothing was sent.

- **calendar** · 2500 bp — Proves a call was scheduled. Does not prove it happened, that it was about this, or that anything was promised on it. Included because on the phone channel it is frequently the only trace there is.



## Metrics

- **promise_keep_rate** (percent) — Share of commitments delivered by the time named. Only honest when the denominator includes promises with no due date recorded — a queue that stops naming times will score perfectly otherwise.

- **silent_break_share** (percent) — Of the promises that broke, the share where nothing went out before the customer noticed. The most diagnostic number in this file and the one most support organisations have never computed, because it requires knowing the promise existed.

- **notice_lead_time** (hours) — How far BEFORE the due time a slip was communicated. Negative values are not notice and should be reported separately rather than averaged in, which is how this metric is usually ruined.

- **renegotiations_per_commitment** (count) — Resets per promise. A team improving its keep-rate while this climbs is not getting more reliable, it is moving the goalposts more skilfully.

- **unrecorded_commitment_rate** (percent) — Promises discovered only because the customer quoted them back at us. Impossible to measure directly and worth estimating anyway, because it is the true size of the gap this object exists to close.

- **time_to_close_the_loop** (hours) — From the due time to the message that actually addressed what was promised. Not to when the work finished.
- **commitments_per_ticket** (count) — How many promises a ticket accumulates. Rising counts usually mean the first promise was not kept, so this reads as a rework metric rather than an engagement one.

## Examples

- **I will check with engineering and come back to you Thursday.** _(typical)_ — The canonical commitment and the reason this object exists. Action, time and owner all present, nothing contractual anywhere near it, and no SLA field in any ticketing system on the market is watching it.

- **I'll come back to you as soon as I know more.** _(misclassification)_ — Not a commitment — no time was named. Recording it as a soft one produces a promise that can never be late and never be discharged. The correct handling is to surface it to the agent as an unfinished sentence, in time for them to finish it in the same reply.

- **No date for the fix yet, but I'll update you Friday either way.** _(edge)_ — Reads as a non-commitment to a careless application of the rule and is in fact the best move in the discipline. The promise is the update, and the update has a time. See the exception.

- **Four-hour SLA met, Thursday callback missed.** _(counterexample)_ — Every contractual clock green, one broken promise, and the customer describes the whole experience as us not getting back to them. The disagreement between the SLA report and the CSAT report is not a measurement error; it is this.

- **Thursday arrived with no news, so nothing was sent.** _(typical)_ — How most commitments actually die. Not neglect and not malice — an agent deciding an update containing no answer was not worth the customer's time.

- **"Thursday, once you send me the logs." The logs never came.** _(misclassification)_ — The overdue detector's standing false accusation. Suppressed by the ball_in_court pattern, which is why that pattern exists and why it is only worth 6500.

- **Wednesday, then Friday, then next week.** _(edge)_ — Each reset defensible in isolation and every one delivered with notice. The sequence is the finding, and it is only visible because renegotiation chains instead of overwriting.

- **Promised on a call, never written down, quoted back six weeks later.** _(edge)_ — The customer is right and we have no record. Treat their memory as the record; the dispute is also the cheapest measurement of how large the capture gap really is.

- **A live promise made to an admin who left the company a month ago.** _(edge)_ — Delivering it now is indistinguishable from silence — the message lands in a dead mailbox and the compliance metric turns green. The promise has to be re-made to a new person, which is a different action entirely.


## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> The most executable object in the Customer Support brain, and the only one where that claim is comfortable. Eleven of eighteen patterns fire against the substrate as it stands: commitment.due_at and commitment.action are real fact paths, followup_sent is a real observation kind, reply_cadence is a real baseline, and commitment_overdue is a real Layer 2 situation type that routes today through customer_support.sit.promised_followup_overdue. Everywhere else in this domain the honest answer is "no support pack exists"; here the honest answer is that the promise-keeping motion is genuinely instrumented, largely by accident, because a commitment extractor was built for a sales pipeline and promises turn out to be domain-neutral.
The three patterns worth acting on first are, in order: commitment.missed_in_silence (a day past a named time with nothing observed outbound — the flagship, and the single most useful alert this brain can currently raise); commitment.due_within_hours_and_still_ours (the pre-breach window, where the fix is free); and commitment.customer_stopped_chasing_after_we_went_quiet (silence after a broken promise read as escalation rather than as acceptance, which is the reading most alerting systems get backwards).
The seven needs_signal patterns are ranked by what they unlock. `callback_promised` is first: today's due dates come from an extractor tuned to sales phrasing, so support wordings — "revert before end of play", "ping you Thursday" — are caught unevenly and, worse, a date the CUSTOMER named can be attributed to us. `commitment_renegotiated` is second and is proposed here rather than taken from planned_substrate, because nothing in that list covers it and the notice-versus-silence distinction is close to the entire value of this object: without it, a team that resets responsibly and a team that slips silently produce identical traces. `commitment.owner` is third, because a promise attached to a thread rather than to a person cannot survive a shift handover.
Two deliberate divergences from the rest of the library, both flagged rather than hidden. (1) The state values `kept`, `missed`, `renegotiated` and `abandoned` are not in vocabulary.yaml open.object_states. `closed` cannot distinguish a promise honoured from a promise quietly dropped, and that distinction is the object. (2) The abandonment threshold is three days where sla-target.yaml uses two for a contractual clock; a personal promise absorbs one working day of slippage without becoming a character question and a contractual one does not. The gap is intentional and should stay intentional.
The arithmetic convention — hours_since a future timestamp is negative, so `> 0` means overdue and `>= -4 AND < 0` means due within four hours — is shared with sla-target.yaml and must not diverge, or the two objects will silently disagree about what overdue means.
